units.title: Europe between 500-1500 C.E
units.intro:
Western Rome collapses (5th c.). Germanic kingdoms, the Church, and Roman memory fill the gap. **Feudalism:** king → lords → knights → peasants / serfs. Land (fief) is paid for with military service. Manors try to be self-sufficient. Church owns land, runs literacy, claims authority over kings (investiture fights).

Franks: Clovis converts; Charlemagne crowned 800, briefly reunites a slice of the west; empire splits. 1215 Magna Carta limits the English king. 1347 Black Death kills a huge share of Europe — labour shortage, shaken faith, faster end of old manorial routines.

cards.title: 1.1 Western Europe (500- 1500 C.E)
body: The period that extends from 500 to 1500 C.E., is known as the Middle Ages or Medieval Period in European history.
The invasions of Germanic tribes, Christianity, and the Roman legacy shaped the history of the Western Europe during the Middle Ages.
A monk is a man who separates himself from ordinary human society in order to lead a life of total dedication to God.
The practice of living the life of a monk is known as monasticism.
Although individual monks were poor and powerless, the monasteries became rich and important institutions, first in the Frankish kingdom and later all over Western Europe.

lessons.title: Byzantine Empire and the Crusades (500- 1500 C.E)

cards.title: 1.2 Byzantine Empire and the Crusades (500- 1500 C.E)
body: From Eastern Roman Empire to Byzantine Empire The Eastern Roman Empire faced many challenges.
At the same time, the Byzantine Empire was built on a Christian faith.

The Byzantine Empire imported goods such as silk from China, spices from southeast Asia and India, jewelry and ivory from India, wheat and furs from Southern Russia, and flax and honey from the Balkans.
The Macedonian dynasty of the tenth and eleventh centuries restored much of the power of the Byzantine Empire.
The greatest challenge came from the advance of the Seljuk Turks who had moved into Asia Minor—the heartland of the Byzantine Empire and its main source of food and workers.

cards.title: Byzantine Empire and the Crusades (500- 1500 C.E)
body: East: Byzantine Empire keeps Roman law and Greek learning, Orthodox Christianity, capital Constantinople. Justinian’s code. Crusades (from 1095): western knights to the Levant — religious zeal, papal politics, Italian trade profits; they wound Byzantium as well as fighting Muslim states. 1453 Constantinople falls to the Ottomans — a date that also opens Unit 9.

cards.title: More notes — medieval Europe
body: After 476 there is no single western emperor. Power becomes local: whoever can feed armed men on a piece of land is a lord. Vassalage is a contract of loyalty, not modern citizenship. The manor grows food, mills grain, holds a court. Towns shrink then slowly return after 1000 with fairs and Italian/Flemish cloth. The Church is the only trans-regional institution — it collects tithe, runs monasteries as memory-banks, and claims the right to crown kings.

East and west drift: Latin vs Greek, pope vs patriarch, 1054 schism. Crusades begin as armed pilgrimage and become colonial toeholds and loot. Fourth Crusade (1204) sacks Christian Constantinople — a wound Byzantium never fully heals. Meanwhile universities (Paris, Bologna) and Gothic cathedrals show the High Middle Ages were not only mud.

tips.text: After the fall of the Roman Empire, Europe was divided into two distinct parts known as Western Europe and Eastern (Byzantine) Roman Empires.
Between 500 and 1500 C.E., both parts passed through two different histories.
The period between 500 and 1500 C.E. in the Western Europe is known as Middle Ages or Medieval Period.
Generally, the Middle Ages was marked by a relatively retarded economic, cultural and intellectual developments, emergence of feudalism, and rise of strong monarchies.
The Middle Ages is generally subdivided into three sub-periods, namely the Early Middle Ages (4761000 C.E.), the High Middle Ages (10001300 C.E.), and the Late Middle Ages (13001450 C.E.).
Between the fifth and eighth centuries C.E., different Germanic tribes created regional kingdoms in present day France, Italy, England, Spain and North Africa.
The Germanic kingdoms in Spain, Italy and North Africa were destroyed by the Byzantine Empire and the Arabs.
Thereafter, the Germanic kingdom in France became the only surviving Germanic kingdom in Western Europe.
The Germanic kingdom in France is known as the Frankish Kingdom.
The kingdom reached its height when Charlemagne came to power. But after Charlemagne’s death, the Frankish Kingdom disintegrated.

units.title: The Rise of Islam, 600 -1500 C.E
units.intro:
7th-century Arabia: towns (Mecca, Medina), clans, long-distance trade. Muhammad’s message: one God, community (umma) over clan. Hijra 622 = year 1 of the Muslim calendar. After his death, the caliphate expands across the Middle East, North Africa, into Iberia and toward Central Asia — speed from mobility, weak neighbours (Byzantium and Persia exhausted), and a unifying faith-and-law.

Umayyads then Abbasids. Baghdad as a learning city: paper, translation of Greek science, algebra, medicine, architecture. Trade stitches the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean. Islam in this unit is a civilization, not only a creed — law, cities, scholarship.

lessons.title: The Arabs and the Rise of Islam

cards.title: 2.1 The Arabs and the Rise of Islam
body: Like the Hebrews and the Assyrians, the Arabs were a Semiticspeaking people who lived in the Arabian Peninsula.
The Arabs lived as farmers and sheepherders on the oases and rain-fed areas of the Arabian Peninsula.
Towns developed along the routes as the Arabs became major carriers of goods between the Indian and the Mediterranean regions.
Most early Arabs were polytheistic—they believed in many gods.
The flight of Mohammed and his followers from Mecca to Medina is known as the Hijrah.

cards.title: 2.2 The Appearance of Islamic Empires
body: Mohammed was both the political and religious leader of the Islamic community.
Shortly after his death in 632, some of his closest followers chose Abu Bakr, a wealthy merchant and Mohammed’s father-in-law, to be their leader.
Under Abu Bakr and his successors, the Islamic movement began to grow, and expanded in Arabia and beyond.
At Yarmuk in 636, the Arab army defeated the Byzantine army.
Four years later, they took control of the Byzantine province of Syria.

cards.title: More notes — Islamic world
body: Mecca’s shrine and caravan wealth made a religious-commercial hub before Islam. The Qur’an and the practice of the Prophet become the reference for law (sharia as an evolving scholarly project, not a single code). After 661 the Umayyads run an Arab-family empire from Damascus; non-Arab converts push back, and the Abbasid revolution (750) moves the centre to Iraq.

The “House of Wisdom” image is a school shorthand for translation and new work in medicine (Ibn Sina), optics (Ibn al-Haytham), and algebra (al-Khwarizmi). Iberia and Sicily later pass some of that into Latin Europe — a bridge into Unit 6. Political unity fractures into many courts; the civilization stays connected by Arabic, law, and trade.

cards.title: 2.3 Islamic Civilizations
body: The Arabs conducted extensive trade, not only within the Islamic world but also with China, the Byzantine Empire, India, Southeast Asia and Africa.
Trade was carried both by ship and by camel caravans.
The Arabs imported gold and slaves from south of the Sahara; silk and porcelain from China; gold and ivory from Eastern Africa; and sandalwood and spices from the lands of Southeast Asia and India.
Within the Arab empire, Egypt contributed grain; Iraq provided linens, dates, and precious stones; and Western India supplied textile goods.
The development of banking and the use of coins made it easier to exchange goods.

glossary.meaning: Those who practice the religion of Islam are called Muslims.
Much of the Sharia'h is drawn from the Quran and from the Hadith, which is a collection of the sayings and activities of the prophet Mohammed.

tips.text: Before the advent of Islam, most early Arabs were polytheistic.
In the fifth and sixth centuries, the economy of the Arabian Peninsula grew.
Despite, economic prosperity, however, Arabian society was extremely unequal. There was a wide gap between the rich and the poor.
The inequality between the rich and the poor, and the greed shown by the wealthy Arabs deeply worried Mohammed.
Mohammed meditated deeply about these issues in the caves of the nearby hills. Then during one of his frequent visits to the caves, Mohammed received revelations from God.
The revelations were eventually written down to form the Quran.
The revelations of Mohammed became the base for a new monotheistic religion called Islam.
The followers of Islam are called Muslims.
Like Christianity and Judaism, Islam is monotheistic.
Islam is not just a set of religious beliefs. It also contains guidelines by which every Muslim is supposed to live. These guidelines are called Shariah laws.

units.title: Civilizations in the Americas, 500 -1500 C.E
units.intro:
No wheel-and-beast package like Eurasia; still cities and states. Mesoamerica: Maya (city-states, writing, calendar, maize), then later Aztec Triple Alliance on Lake Texcoco — tribute empire, chinampas, Tenochtitlán. Andes: Inca road-and-storehouse state, terraces, quipu records, Cuzco. Environment writes the rules: rainforest vs high dry mountains.

These worlds meet Europe after 1492 (Unit 7) — disease and steel hit them hard. Know them first as civilizations on their own terms.

cards.title: 3.1 Early Civilizations in Mesoamerica
body: The two most important civilizations to emerge in Mesoamerica were the Mayan and Aztec civilizations.
The Mayan civilization flourished between 300 and 900 C.E on the Yucatán Peninsula.
The Maya built splendid temples and pyramids and developed a complicated calendar.
Mayan civilization came to include much of Central America and Southern Mexico.
Mayan civilization was composed of city-states, each governed by a hereditary ruling class.

cards.title: More notes — Americas
body: Maize domestication is the long preface: surplus allows cities. Maya writing records dynastic war as well as ritual astronomy; collapse of some classic cities is a lesson in drought plus politics, not “mystery vanished people.” Aztec power is a late, intense tribute machine — flower wars and sacrifice are part of state ideology and intimidation, which Spanish writers then exaggerate for their own ends. Read both.

Inca: no phonetic writing, but the state still runs a census-like labour draft (mit’a) and food stores against Andean frost. Roads are political control. When Pizarro arrives, a succession war is already open — conquest is not only 168 Spaniards being magical.

cards.title: 3.2 Early Civilizations in South America
body: In the late 1300s, the Inca were only a small community in the area of Cuzco, a city located high in the mountains of Southern Peru.
In the 1440s, however, under the leadership of the powerful ruler Pachacuti, the Incas brought the entire region under their control, and thus formed an empire.
Pachacuti and his immediate successors extended the boundaries of the Incan Empire as far as Ecuador, central Chile, and the edge of the Amazon basin.
The empire included about twelve million people.
By and large, the Incan state was a result of war.

tips.text: Between 400 and 1500 C.E., the Mayan, Aztec, and Incan civilizations emerged in the Americas. These civilizations developed very complex societies with well developed government systems, cultures, and buildings.
The Mayan, Aztec and Incan civilizations had monarchical governments and their economies were largely based on agriculture.
All of them undertook big building projects which included the building of temples, palaces and pyramids.
The people of these civilizations were polytheistic. But the most important god was the sun god. Moreover, all these civilizations practiced human sacrifice on a large scale.
The Mayan civilization collapsed in the 8th and 9th centuries C.E.
The causes for the decline of the Mayan civilization were natural disasters, such as diseases and soil exhaustion, peasant revolt, and foreign invasions.
The causes for the final demise of the Aztec and Incan civilizations were the same. Both flourishing civilizations were brought to an end due to Spanish conquests.

The Spaniards caused the collapse of both civilizations in two ways: they brought with them smallpox that devastated the peoples of the Americas, and they militarily conquered these peoples and eventually colonized them for more than three hundred years (from 16th to 19th centuries).

units.title: Civilizations in Sub- Saharan Africa
units.intro:
States grow on trade and iron. East Africa: Swahili coast — city-states (Kilwa, Mombasa) linking inland gold/ivory to Indian Ocean merchants; Islam as a commercial-language layer. West Africa: Ghana, then Mali (gold–salt, Timbuktu, Mansa Musa), then Songhai — control of savannah routes. Central: forest kingdoms (Kongo later). South: Great Zimbabwe — stone enclosure, gold toward the coast.

Africa in this book is not a blank waiting for Europe. Unit 7’s slave trade hits already-complex societies.

lessons.title: Rise of Civilizations in Sub-Saharan Africa

cards.title: 4.1 Rise of Civilizations in Sub-Saharan Africa
body: Africa is believed to be the birthplace of humanity.
The earliest peoples of Africa supported themselves by hunting and gathering.
Around 5000 B.C.E. crop farming and animal husbandry were introduced to the North African coastal regions, probably from Western Asia.

cards.title: 4.2 East Africa
body: In Eastern Africa, a variety of states and small societies took root.
Islam also strongly influenced many of them.
In East Africa, the Bantus gradually began to participate in the sea trade along the East African coast.
With the rise of Islam in the seventh and eigth centuries C.E., the Eastern coast of Africa became an important part of the trading network along the Indian Ocean.
Beginning in the eighth century, Muslims from the Arabian Peninsula and the Persian Gulf began to settle at ports along the Indian coast.

cards.title: 4.3 West Africa
body: By 750 C.E., camels were widely used in the trans-Saharan trade as major transport vehicle.
The expansion of the trans-Saharan trade had led to the emergence of market centers and finally the civilizations of West Africa.
Ghana, the first great trading state in West Africa, emerged as early as 500 C.E.
The kingdom of Ghana was located in the upper Niger River valley, a grassland region between the Sahara and the tropical forests along the West African coast.
The capital of the Ghanaian kingdom was at Kumbi Saleh.

cards.title: More notes — Africa south of the Sahara
body: Sahara is a sea of camels after the 7th–8th centuries: gold south, salt and horses north, Islam riding with merchants. Ghana (in the older savannah sense, not the modern republic’s borders) taxes the trade; Mali’s mansas do the same on a larger Niger-bend stage; Songhai’s army and river fleet try to hold it. When firearms and new Atlantic options arrive (Unit 7), that inland system is shaken.

Swahili culture is African and Indian-Ocean at once — language Bantu-based, architecture coral-stone, religion Islam in the towns. Great Zimbabwe’s walls are local granite skill, not a “foreign mystery.” Always reject the empty-continent myth with a named city.

cards.title: 4.4 Central Africa
body: The Lake Kisale region, which is found in the southeast of modern Democratic Republic of Congo, had been inhabited by iron-making farmers since the fourth century C.E.
The region was good for agriculture, fishing and hunting.
Over the centuries, the peoples of the region known as Luba developed sophisticated agriculture and learnt the techniques of drying fish.
By 1300 C.E., the Luba were organized into a number of prosperous farming and trading chiefdoms.
Between 1300 and 1400 C.E., these chiefdoms were organized into a single centralized kingdom under a dynasty known as Nkongolo.

cards.title: 4.5 Southern Africa
body: In the Southern half of the African continent, states formed more slowly than in the north.
Until the eleventh century C.E., most of the peoples in this region lived in independent villages organized by clans and led by a local rulers or clan heads.
In the grassland regions south of the Zambezi River, a mixed economy of farming, cattle herding, and trade had developed over a period of many centuries.
Villages in this area were usually built inside walls to protect the domestic animals from wild animals at night.
Beginning in the eleventh century, in some parts of Southern Africa, these independent villages gradually began to unite and establish the first states.

tips.text: By around 200 C.E., the Bantu speaking peoples of West Africa grew in number due to growth in food production.
The increase in population put pressure on the available land and water. Therefore, the Bantus began to migrate to Central, Eastern, and Southern parts of Africa.

The Bantus brought with them the knowledge of agriculture and iron-making. They created agricultural villages and introduced new social organizations. This laid the foundation for the emergence of states and empires in Sub-Saharan Africa.
In East Africa, states were established in the Lakes Region and Eastern Coastal areas.
The states of East Africa were mainly the result of interactions between the indigenous communities, the Bantus, and Muslims from the Arabian Peninsula.
The states of the Lake Region were predominantly agricultural.
The major states of the region were Bunyoro, Ankole, and Buganda.
Whereas, the coastal states, also known as Swahili states, were largely dependent on trade.
The Swahili states had a series of ports such as Mogadishu, Mombasa, and Kilwa. They also developed a rich culture; combining African, Arabic and Islamic traditions.
The states in West Africa were largely the result of the trans-Saharan trade.

units.title: Asia between 400 and 1500 C.E
units.intro:
China reunifies after Han fragments: Sui then Tang then Song — exams, canals, urban commerce, gunpowder, print, compass. Mongols under Chinggis and successors create a vast land empire; Yuan dynasty in China; overland peace of sorts for merchants; then Ming restores a Chinese house and later limits official maritime reach.

Japan: borrows writing and Buddhism from the continent, then samurai / shogun pattern, less central exam-state than China. Korea as a bridge culture. India after Guptas: regional kingdoms, then incoming Islamic sultanates in the north — stage-set for Mughals (Unit 9).

cards.title: 5.1 The Reunification of China
body: The Han dynasty came to an end in 220 C.E., and China fell into disorder.
For the next three hundred years, the Chinese suffered disorder and civil war.
The Sui dynasty (581–618) did not last long, but it managed to unify China once again under the emperor’s authority.
The Sui dynasty declined during the reign of Sui Yangdi, the second emperor of the dynasty.
The Grand Canal, which was built to link the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers, is the world’s longest canal, extending for 1900kms.

cards.title: 5.2 The Mongols and China
body: The Mongols were a pastoral people from the region of modernday Mongolia who were organized loosely into clans.
In 1206, Temujin was elected Genghis Khan (“strong ruler”) by the Mongols.
From that time on, the Mongols under Genghis Khan expanded their control almost all over Asia and some parts of Europe.
The Mongols brought much of East and Southwest Asia and Central Europe under a single rule.
The Mongol empire was the largest land empire in history.

cards.title: 5.3 Japan and Korea
body: The ancestors of present-day Japan settled in the Yamato Plain near the modern cities of Osaka and Kyoto in the first centuries C.E.
The people were divided between a small aristocratic ruling class and a large population of rice farmers, artisans, and household servants.
The local ruler of each clan protected the population in return for a share of the annual produce.
In the early Seventh century C.E, a prince named Shotoku Taishi, , tried to unify the various clans in order to defend Japan from Chinese invasion.
Prince Shotoku created a new centralized system of government in Japan, based roughly on the Chinese model.

cards.title: 5.4 India After the Guptas
body: In the mid-fifth century, for example, the Huns, a nomadic people from Central Asia, invaded India.
The Huns invaded India again in 510 C.E., and succeeded in pushing the Guptas into the northeast.
The Huns were thus able to control much of northeast India.
Eventually, the Hun Kingdom and the Gupta Empire collapsed in 550 C.E.
The collapse of the Hun Kingdom and the Gupta Empire gave rise to the emergence of independent regional kingdoms.

cards.title: More notes — Asia 400–1500
body: Tang China is cosmopolitan (Chang’an, Silk Road, Buddhism). Song is poorer in cavalry but richer in markets, paper money experiments, and scholar-officials. The Mongol century is destruction then a Pax on the steppe routes; it also moves engineers and plague. Ming restoration is proud and wary — later official voyages stop, but private coastal trade does not simply die.

Japan’s borrowing is selective: they take characters and Buddhism, not the full Chinese exam-empire. Warrior houses fill the gap of a weak centre until a shogun freezes the game (Unit 10). India is many regions: temple states in the south, Turkic-Afghan sultanates in the north — Persianate court culture sitting on a Hindu-majority countryside. That mix is the runway for the Mughals.

tips.text: Between 400 and 1500 C.E., many developments occurred in Asia, especially in China, Japan, Korea, and India.
After the Han dynasty collapsed in 220 C.E., three hundred years of disorder and civil war followed.
The period of disorder and war ended in the sixth century, and three successive dynasties came to power. These were the Sui, Tang, and Song dynasties.
During the reign of the three dynasties, China was once again unified under one government and many other advances were made.
In the thirteenth century, however, China was invaded by the Mongols.
The Mongols overthrew the Song dynasty and created their own dynasty.
The Mongols, under their famous leader Genghis Khan and his sons, created the largest empire in history.
The Mongols brought economic prosperity and stability to China.
Eventually, however, Mongol rule in China declined in the fourteenth century. It was replaced by a new Chinese dynasty known as Ming.
Japan’ history was influenced by its geography.

units.title: Renaissance and Reformation
units.intro:
Renaissance: rebirth of classical art and inquiry, starting in rich Italian cities (Florence, Venice, Rome) — patronage, perspective, human dignity in this world (humanism), print spreads books. Not a clean break: still Christian Europe, still plague memories.

Reformation: Luther 1517 challenges indulgences and papal authority — scripture in the vernacular, salvation by faith. Princes pick sides (land and power as well as belief). Calvin, English break under Henry VIII. Catholic reform (Council of Trent) answers. Europe splits confessionally — fuse to Unit 8 wars of religion.

cards.title: 6.1 The Renaissance
body: The period of European history from 1350 to 1550 is called the Renaissance.
Historians called this period the Renaissance because the period witnessed a rebirth of interest in ancient Greek and Roman civilizations.
The revival was related to art, literature, architecture, and culture.
The Renaissance marked a new age totally different from the Middle Ages.
The Renaissance has been described as ending the medieval era and marking the start of the modern age.

cards.title: 6.2 The Protestant Reformation
body: The Protestant Reformation is the name given to the religious reform movement to correct certain practices and doctrines of the Roman Catholic Church.
The Reformation established many protestant sects.
A protestant means a person who oppose to the Roman Catholic or Eastern Orthodox faith.
In Western Europe the reformation divided the Catholic Church into Catholic and Protestant groups, which increased Christian diversity.
The causes of the Reformation were mainly related with church abuse and the decline of the prestige of the church.

cards.title: More notes — Renaissance and Reformation
body: Italian bankers and popes buy art that looks at living bodies and Roman ruins. Northern Europe adds oil paint and a more urban piety. Humanists want better Latin and Hebrew texts — that textual itch also produces better Bibles, which is why print + humanism + a corrupt-indulgence spark can become Luther.

Reformation is political geography: a German prince who becomes Lutheran keeps monastery land; a Spanish king stays Catholic and builds an overseas empire as champion of Rome. Ordinary people meet the change as a new sermon language, a smashed statue, or a neighbour denounced. Wars of religion in Unit 8 are this unit with armies.

glossary.meaning: The Protestant Reformation is the name given to the religious reform movement to correct certain practices and doctrines of the Roman Catholic Church.

tips.text: The Italian Renaissance followed on the period of the Middle Ages and was characterized by the birth of Humanism, which emphasized the importance of individual achievement in a wide range of fields.
Under the influence of the Humanists, literature and the arts climbed to new levels.
Though it eventually spread through Europe, the Renaissance began in the city-states of Italy.
Italian merchants and political officials supported and commissioned the great artists of the day, thus the products of the Renaissance grew up inside their walls.
The most powerful city-states were Florence, the Papal States (centered in Rome), Venice, and Milan.

Florence, considered the birthplace of the Renaissance, grew powerful as a wool-trading post and remained powerful throughout the Renaissance due to the leadership of the Medici family, who maintained the city's financial strength and were generous patrons of the arts.
Venice and Milan also grew wealthy and powerful, playing large roles in Italian politics and attracting many artists and writers.
Venice was ruled by oligarchy in the hands of its Great Council of noble families and Milan by a strong monarchy that produced a line of powerful dukes.
Perhaps the most prominent feature of the Renaissance was the furthering of the arts and the advancement of new techniques and styles.

The pick of artistic talent and production came during what is known as the High Renaissance, in the form of Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael, and Michaelangelo, who remain the best known artists of the Renaissance.

units.title: European Exploration and the African slave trade 1500–1800
units.intro:
Motives: gold, God, glory, plus a way to Asia that skips Ottoman-controlled land routes. Portuguese down Africa to India; Spanish west into the Americas. Compass, caravel, guns. Consequence: Columbian exchange (crops, animals, diseases), silver to Europe and China, collapse of Aztec and Inca power, plantation complex.

Atlantic slave trade: European demand for labour on sugar/tobacco/cotton; African brokers and wars feed captives; Middle Passage; huge demographic and social cost in parts of West and Central Africa. This is not the first slavery in history — it is a new scale, racialised, and tied to capital across an ocean.

cards.title: 7.1 European Expansion
body: Economic reasons were the main motives for European expansion.
In the fourteenth century, conquests by the Ottoman Turks reduced the ability of Westerners to travel by land to the East.
Europeans were looking for access to Asia by sea.
Merchants, adventurers, and state officials had high hopes of expanding trade, especially for the spices of the East.
The spices, which were needed to preserve and flavor food, were very expensive after being shipped to Europe by Arab middlemen.

lessons.title: Africa during the Era of the Slave Trade

cards.title: 7.2 Africa during the Era of the Slave Trade
body: Early European explorers sought gold in Africa but were soon involved in the slave trade.
The exchange of slaves became an important part of European trade.
As in other areas of the world, slavery had been practiced in Africa since ancient times.
In the fifteenth century, it continued to be practiced.
The primary market for African slaves was the land of Arabia, where most slaves were used as domestic servants.

cards.title: More notes — oceans and slaving
body: Iberian ports sit at the right corner of winds and of a crusading-reconquest mindset. Once American silver and sugar exist, the Dutch, English and French muscle in. Indigenous labour dies too fast for the mines and mills, so planters buy enslaved Africans. The triangle (manufactures → Africa, people → Americas, sugar/silver → Europe) is a diagram — real ships also ran other legs.

Demographic shock in the Americas is the largest single fact. In West Africa the shock is different: guns-for-people, skewed sex ratios in some zones, new slaving states, and inland societies that refuse or flee. Write both continents; do not make Africa only a reservoir.

tips.text: In the fourteenthcentury Europe was in search of a sea trade route to India. Thus, an economic reason was the main factor for European exploration.
Portugal took the lead in exploring the coast of Africa under the sponsorship of Prince Henry the Navigator, the youngest son of the Portuguese king, John I.
In 1488, Bartholomew Diaz reached the Southern tip of Africa, the Cape of Good Hope.
In 1497-1498, Vasco da Gama rounded the Cape and sailed to India. He returned with a cargo worth sixty times the cost of the voyage. His trip caused anxiety in Western Europe.
Spain financed two significant expeditions.
In 1492, Christopher Columbus, an Italian navigator, sailed from Spain.

Convinced that the earth is round, Columbus planned to reach the East by sailing Westward across the Atlantic Ocean. He failed because his ships were blocked by two continents up to then unknown to Europe.
Although Columbus thought he had reached the islands off the coast of Asia, he had actually come to what Europeans later considered to be a new world.
Because this region was publicized by the European explorer, Amerigo Vespucci, it was later named the America.

In 1519 Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese sea captain, led several ships from Spain to circumnavigate the world. He rounded the Southern tip of South America and crossed the Pacific but was killed in the Philippine Islands.

units.title: Europe from 1550-1715
units.intro:
Wars of religion after the Reformation (France, Thirty Years’ War 1618–48 — devastates German lands; Westphalia 1648 starts talking about state sovereignty). Prices rise with American silver; peasants and towns strain. Absolutism: monarch claims undivided power — Louis XIV as the school portrait (“l’état c’est moi” image), Versailles, standing army, bureaucracy. England takes another road: civil war, limited monarchy after 1688.

Art and political thought: baroque display; writers arguing divine right vs contract. Stage-set for Unit 11 Enlightenment.

cards.title: 8.1 The Wars of Religion
body: Economic, social, and political forces were the underlying causes of the European religious wars in the sixteenth century.
Out of many other religious wars, the French civil wars known as the French Wars of Religion (1562–1598) and were the most destructive.
The French kings persecuted Protestants, but the persecution did little to stop the spread of Protestantism.
Huguenots were French Protestants influenced by John Calvin.
Towns and provinces, which had long resisted the growing power of the French monarchy were willing to assist nobles in weakening the monarchy.

cards.title: 8.2 War,Revolution,Socio-economic crisis
body: From 1560 to 1650, Europe witnessed severe economic and social crisis.
One major economic problem was inflation – or rising prices.
The great influx of gold and silver from the Americas was one factor.
Population grew in the sixteenth century.
By 1650, population had begun to decline, especially in central and Southern Europe.

cards.title: 8.3 The Rise of Absolute Monarchies
body: One response to the religious wars and socio-economic crises of the seventeenth century was to seek more stability by increasing the power of the monarch.
The result was the rise of absolutism in Europe.
Absolutism is a system of government in which a ruler holds total power.
In seventeenth century Europe, absolutism was based on the idea of the divine right of kings.
Absolute monarchs had tremendous powers.

cards.title: More notes — after 1550
body: Westphalia does not invent the modern state overnight, but textbooks use it as the moment when “whose realm, his religion” and non-interference among princes become speakable. France exits the wars centralised; the Holy Roman Empire stays a puzzle of pieces.

Absolutism is a project, never total: Louis XIV still bargains with tax farmers and grain riots. England’s 1688 settlement is a property-and-parliament deal as much as a liberty hymn. Use both as types, not as cartoons of “tyranny vs freedom.”

lessons.title: The development of art and political thought

cards.title: 8.4 The development of art and political thought
body: Renaissance art came to an end when a new movement, called Mannerism, emerged in Italy in the 1520s and 1530s.
During this period, artists were using elongated figures in their paintings.
Mannerism was eventually replaced by a new movement called the Baroque.
The Baroque painting style was known for its use of dramatic effects to arouse the emotions.
Baroque churches and palaces were magnificent and richly detailed.

glossary.meaning: Absolutism is a system of government in which a ruler holds total power.

tips.text: Different wars were fought in connection with the Protestant Reformation.
The French wars were the most destructive ones.
The wars went on for 30 years until the rights of Protestants were recognized by an edict of the king.
The Protestant Dutch revolted against their Catholic rulers.
Philip II of Spain, after ruthlessly trying to suppress Protestantism in Holland, ultimately failed.
The Dutch led by William of Orange drove out the Spanish forces and, in 1581, declared their political and religious independence.
In 1648 after more fighting, Spain recognized Dutch independence.
Philip II of Spain also planned to invade England, and he organized a huge war fleet, the Spanish Armada.
In 1588, the Armada was sighted off the English coast and destroyed by the English navy.
Religious disputes continued in Germany after the Peace of Augsburg in 1555. Thus, the peace agreement was followed by the Thirty Years’ War.

units.title: The Muslim Empires
units.intro:
Three gunpowder empires. **Ottomans:** take Constantinople 1453, Balkans and Arab lands, millet system, janissaries, Suleiman’s century. **Safavids:** Persia, Shi’a identity as state glue, clash with Ottomans. **Mughals:** Babur into India, Akbar’s wide alliance and administration, later Aurangzeb and strain; Taj Mahal as wealth-and-faith stone.

They are early-modern states: cannon, tax records, court culture — not “medieval leftovers.”

cards.title: 9.1 Ottoman Turkey
body: In the late thirteenth century, a new group of Turks under their leader Osman began to build power in the northwest corner of the Anatolian Peninsula.
At first, the Ottoman Turks were relatively peaceful and engaged in pastoral activities.
In the foureenth century, the Ottoman Turks expanded into the Balkans.
The Byzantine Empire had controlled this area for centuries.
Ottoman rulers claimed the title of sultan and began to build a strong military by developing an elite guard called Janissaries.

cards.title: 9.2 The Rise of Safavid dynasty
body: After the collapse of the empire of Timur Lenk (Tamerlane) in the early fifteenth century, the area extending from Persia into central Asia fell into anarchy (lawlessness and disorder).
Unlike many of their Islamic neighbors who were Sunni Muslims, the Safavids were Shiites.
The Safavid dynasty was founded by Shah Ismail, the descendant of Safi al-Din (after whom the name Safavid came from).
In the early fourteenth century, Safi al-Din was the leader of a community of Turkish ethnic groups in Azerbaijan, near the Caspian Sea.
In 1501, Ismail used his forces to seize much of Iran and Iraq.

cards.title: 9.3 Mogul India
body: In 1500, the Indian subcontinent was still divided into a number of Hindu and Muslim kingdoms.
The Moguls were not natives of India, but came from the mountainous region north of the Indus River valley.
The founder of the Mogul dynasty was Babur.
Babur had inherited a part of Timur Lenk’s empire.
Thirteen years later, his forces entered India.

cards.title: More notes — gunpowder empires
body: Ottomans sit on the old Roman/Byzantine road from Balkans to Arab lands; controlling the eastern Mediterranean and the Red Sea approaches makes them a European *and* an Asian power. Devshirme and timar land-grants are how a peasant empire pays a professional army before full cash taxes.

Safavid Iran makes Shi’a identity a border against the Ottomans — religion as geopolitics. Mughals rule a majority-non-Muslim population: Akbar’s alliances are statecraft; later more rigid policy is also statecraft, with different costs. All three courts speak a culture of Persian letters even when the army speaks Turkish or other tongues.

tips.text: The Ottoman, Safavid and Moghal empires, which were founded between 1453 and 1526, formed the three great Muslim empires of the early modern period.
By the early seventeenth century they controlled territories which stretched from the Balkans and North Africa in the West to Bengal and South India in the East.
The three empires represented the last period of Islamic civilization, which was overwhelmed by the onset from the late eighteenth century of Western power.
The empires were able to conquer vast territory in Europe and Asia using firearms.
Religion played a major ideological role in the establishment of the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mogul Empires.
Trade and the arts flourished under the three Muslim empires.

units.title: China, Japan and Korea from 1400 to 1800
units.intro: Ming then Qing (Manchu) China: huge agrarian empire, examination elite, porcelain and tea in world trade, official caution about open coasts after early voyages. Tokugawa Japan: after civil war, shogunate freezes society, controls daimyo, limits foreign entry (except a Dutch window at Nagasaki) — long internal peace and urban culture. Korea: Joseon state, Chinese-inspired exams, survives between giants.

cards.title: 10.1 China at Its Height
body: A new dynasty, the Ming dynasty began to rule China.
The founder of the new dynasty took the title of Ming Emperor.
After his death, his son Yong Le became emperor.
In 1406, Yong Le began construction of the Imperial City in Beijing.
In 1421 he moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing.

cards.title: 10.2 Tokugawa Japan and Korea
body: At the end of the fifteenth century, Japan was in chaos.
The centralized power of the shogunate had collapsed.
Heads of noble families called daimyo controlled their own lands and were at war with their neighbors.
The process of unification began in the late sixteenth century with three powerful political leaders.
Nobunaga seized the imperial capital of Kyoto and placed the reigning shogun under his control.

cards.title: More notes — East Asia 1400–1800
body: Qing expansion into Inner Asia makes a land empire as impressive as any European sea empire — just pointed inward. The exam system keeps the Han elite cooperating. Population growth strains land; silver from Japan and then from Spanish America pays taxes — East Asia is already in a global money web.

Tokugawa peace is real: castles freeze, samurai become paid officials who still wear two swords. Merchant wealth in Osaka and Edo sits awkwardly under a status system that says merchants are low. When American ships force doors in the 1850s (next grade), that tension explodes. Korea’s Joseon hangs on Confucian order and pays dearly when neighbours modernise first.

tips.text: The Ming Dynasty was the ruling dynasty of China for 276 years (1368–1644) following the collapse of the Mongol-led Yuan Dynasty. the Ming capital Beijing fell in 1644 to a rebellion led by Li Zicheng (who established the Shun Dynasty, soon replaced by the Manchu-led Qing Dynasty).

Ming rule saw enormous construction projects, including the restoration of the Grand Canal and the Great Wall and the establishment of the Forbidden City in Beijing during the first quarter of the fifteenth century.
Ming rulers attempted to create a society of self-sufficient rural communities in a rigid, immobile system that would have no need to engage with the commercial life and trade of urban centers.
China became involved in a new global trade of goods, plants, animals, and food crops.
Trade with European powers and the Japanese brought in massive amounts of silver.

During the last decades of the Ming, the flow of silver into China diminished greatly, undermining state revenues. This damage to the Ming economy was compounded by the effects on agriculture, natural calamities, crop failure, and sudden epidemics.
The ensuing breakdown of authority and people's livelihoods allowed rebel leaders to challenge Ming authority.
The Qing Dynasty was the last imperial dynasty of China, ruling from 1644 to 1912.
The dynasty was founded by the Manchu in contemporary NorthEastern China.
Over the course of its reign, the Qing became highly integrated with Chinese culture.

units.title: The Scientific Revolution and The Enlightenment
units.intro:
Scientific Revolution: question inherited authority by observation and maths. Copernicus (sun-centred), Galileo (telescope, conflict with church courts), Newton (laws, gravity) — a mechanical clockwork cosmos. Method: hypothesis, measure, publish.

Enlightenment: apply reason to society. Locke (rights, consent), Montesquieu (separation of powers), Rousseau (general will — handle with care), Voltaire (tolerance, anti-fanaticism). Salons, print, coffee-houses. Enlightened monarchs borrow useful bits (tax, army, schools) without giving away the throne. Ideas travel toward Atlantic revolutions (Grade 11).

cards.title: 11.1 The Scientific Revolution
body: In the Middle Ages, many educated Europeans became more interested in the world around them.
A number of changes in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries made the natural philosophers abandon their old views and develop new ones.
First, Renaissance humanists had mastered Greek as well as Latin and thus had access to newly discovered works by Ptolemy, Archimedes, and Plato.
The invention of new instruments, such as the telescope and microscope, also made fresh scientific discoveries possible.
Third, the printing press helped spread new ideas quickly and easily.

cards.title: 11.2 The Enlightenment
body: The Enlightenment was an eighteenth-century philosophical movement of intellectuals who were greatly impressed with the achievements of the Scientific Revolution.
One of the favorite words of these intellectuals was reason.
By this they meant the application of the scientific method to an understanding of all life.
The Enlightenment was especially influenced by the ideas of two seventeenth century Englishmen, Isaac Newton and John Locke.
To Newton, the physical world and everything in it was like a giant machine (the Newtonian world-machine).

cards.title: More notes — reason and nature
body: The new science does not kill religion overnight. Many pioneers are believers who think God wrote two books — scripture and nature. The fight is over who reads nature and whether a telescope can outrank a verse. Newton’s world is lawful; Enlightenment writers ask why law should not also bind kings.

Ideas travel unevenly. A Prussian king funds academies and still runs a parade-ground state. Atlantic revolutionaries quote Locke and still hold slaves. Your essay should praise the tools (evidence, rights language) and still notice who was left outside the “we.”

lessons.title: Political ideas and European politics and in the age of the Enlightenment

cards.title: 11.3 Political ideas and European politics and in the age of the Enlightenment
body: Enlightenment thought had an effect on the political life of European states in the eigthteenth century.
To achieve this, most philosophers believed that people must be governed by enlightened rulers.
In 1740, a major war broke out in connection with the succession to the Austrian throne.
When the Austrian emperor Charles VI died, he was succeeded by his daughter, Maria Theresa.
King Frederick II of Prussia took advantage of the succession of a woman to the throne of Austria by invading Austrian Silesia.

tips.text: The Scientific Revolution brought Europeans a new way of viewing the universe and their place in it.
The Scientific Revolution questioned and ultimately challenged conceptions and beliefs about nature.
It also popularized in the eigthteenth century Enlightenment and the philosophical movement that greatly affected the development of science during the late 1600’s and 1700’s.
The scientists of this period relied heavily on the scientific method, with its emphasis on experimentation and careful observation.
The period also produced many important advances in such fields as Anatomy, Chemistry, Mathematics, and Physics.
Most important of all, the scientists disproved the old thoughts and principles.
Rational thinking was brought about by the Scientific Revolution in Europe.
Scientific Revolution destroyed the ancient and medieval concepts and gave birth to a new outlook based on logical reasoning.
The Enlightenment was an eigthteenth-century philosophical movement of intellectuals who were greatly impressed with the achievements of the Scientific Revolution.
Many of the major Enlightenment thinkers, or philosophes, were French with some English ones.

units.title: Italian colonization in Eritrea
units.intro:
Late 19th-c. Italy is a new nation hunting prestige and a place in the African scramble. Red Sea ports already sit in Ottoman / Egyptian / local power games; Italy picks a foothold at Assab then Massawa and pushes onto the plateau. Adwa 1896 stops Italy in Ethiopia — Eritrea remains the colony they keep.

Policies: racial hierarchy, land alienation for settlers, pass-like controls, limited schooling aimed at clerks not equals. Resistance: local armed refusals, flight, later political organisation (the book’s named episodes — learn those proper nouns from the pages). Economy: ports, railway toward the highland, cash crops and labour for Italian farms and the state; some infrastructure that later Eritreans also use, built first for colonial extraction and settlement.

cards.title: 12.1 Motives of Italian colonialism
body: Italian colonial motives were similar to those of the other European imperialist nations.
At a time when colonies were considered a mark of prestige, Italy became interested in achieving this status like the big powers of Europe.
The combination of this factors influenced Italian colonial expansion in Eritrea.
Between 1861 and 1911, the Italian population increased significantly (from 25 million to 35).
Italy was looking for new settlement areas outside its territory.

cards.title: 12.2 Italian colonial policies
body: Italian colonial policies and practices in Eritrea changed from time to time according to Italian interests and new developments within Eritrea.
Generally, these policies and practices could be seen in three phases.
The First Phase (1890-1896) In this phase, Italian colonialism focused on creating a settler colony in Eritrea.
Within two years 400,000 hectares of land was confiscated.
The opposition forced the colonizers to accept that the policy of settlement was not feasible.

cards.title: 12.3 Eritrean resistance to Italian rule
body: During the advent of the Italians in Eritrea there was no significant resistance from the Eritrean people.
On the contrary, Eritrean notables initially collaborated with the Italians in order to get protection from Tigrean-Amhara and Mahadist raids or to get firearms.
In spite of collaboration they got from the Eritrean local chiefs, the Italians saw the chiefs as potential sources of resistance to their colonial rule and decided to neutralize and weaken them.
Guided by this policy, in the period from 1889-1890, Italy killed hundreds of notables with their followers and imprisoned many others in Asab and the notorious prison island of Nakura.
The leaders of the resistance were the local chiefs because of their leading positions in the traditional society.

cards.title: 12.4 Italian Colonial Rule in Eritrea
body: The first move of the Italians after declaring Eritrea a colony was to set up a stable colonial administration that would enable them to implement their plans.
A preliminary administrative and law enforcement system was introduced.
The setting up of Italian administration in Eritrea had clear objectives of consolidating colonial rule and implementing colonial policies.
In the highlands, existing administrative structures were adopted with some changes or completely replaced.
With the intent of securing the loyalty of local administrators, the Italians appointed traditional chiefs who were closely controlled by Italian administrators (commissari).

cards.title: 12.5 Italian Colonial Economic Activities
body: As stated before limited economic changes took place in the pre1935 period.
The main economic project in that period was the construction of a 248 km long Massawa-Aqordet (Bisha) railway line.
Most of the economic projects were introduced in the post1935 period and were mainly related to strategic military interests of Italy.
Modern infrastructural networks and ports, different factories, modern urban centers with facilities, some mining activities, etc. were established in Eritrea.
Between 1890 and 1941 a total of 710km long all-weather roads had been constructed in Eritrea.

cards.title: Italian Colonial Economic Activities
body: Write this unit without flattening Eritreans into either only victims or only collaborators. Elites, peasants, pastoralists and towns chose under pressure.

cards.title: Exam spine
body: Motives (prestige, strategy, settlers) → how they ruled (law, land, race) → who resisted and how → what the colonial economy built and broke. Dates: Assab/Massawa foothold, 1890 colony name, 1896 Adwa next door, fascist years if the chapter reaches them.

cards.title: More notes — Italy in Eritrea
body: Italy arrives late to the scramble and treats the Red Sea as a shortcut to prestige after unification. Local politics are already layered: Ottoman claims, Egyptian interludes, highland–lowland authority, and trading houses at Massawa. Italians exploit splits; they do not step onto an empty shore.

Colonial rule means maps, courts, and a colour line. Settler agriculture wants highland land already in use. The railway and roads move troops first. Some Eritreans work inside the system (interpreters, soldiers, contractors) because that is how families eat under occupation; others fight or leave. A good answer names both without preaching.

Adwa is Ethiopian victory and Italian humiliation — it freezes Eritrea as the colony Italy can still show on the map. Fascist years (1930s) add harsher race law and the 1935–36 war next door. World War II then breaks the Italian empire; the next textbook picks up British military administration.

tips.text: The advent of Italian colonization in Eritrea was part of the processes of the Scramble for Africa.
Italians gained a foothold in Eritrea by acquiring Assab (1869). They occupied Massawa in 1885 when it was vacated by the Egyptians.
Next, the Italians expanded in various directions of Eritrea. Thus, in 1890, Eritrea became an Italian colony.
Emperor Yohannes as well as Menelik of Abyssinia were also interested in expanding into Eritrea.
Following the Italian defeat at the Battle of Adwa (1896), Ethiopia re-affirmed Italian possessions in Eritrea.
Italian colonial land expropriation policy, among other reasons, brought resentment among the Eritrean people and resulted in resistance from different parts of Eritrea against the colonial rule.
Italy’s rule in Eritrea was designed to establish direct control over the people and its social and economic policies were shaped by Italian economic and military considerations.
Finally Italian rule came to an end in the context of Second World War with British takeover of Eritrea.
The end of Italian colonialism in Eritrea will be dealt in grade 11.
